decision.quote:
Therefore, we compared the correlations computed
based on mean scores to previous findings (Table 5), which
showed by and large similar patterns and correlations as in
previous studies (Delsing et al., 2008; George et al., 2007;
Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003; Zweigenhaft, 2008). In accordance with these studies, correlation analyses as well as the
SEM analysis showed that the personality dimensions
Openness and Extraversion are the best predictors of music
preferences. Further, on the basis of the STOMP dimensions as well as on the soundfiles the present study also
replicated the finding that Openness is positively correlated
to R&C and I&R music, and also that Extraversion is positively related to E&R types of music. Moreover, Rentfrow
and Gosling’s (2003) and Zweigenhaft’s (2008) finding
that Openness is negatively associated with U&C was replicated, as well as that Conscientiousness is negatively correlated with I&R (see Delsing et al., 2008; George et al.,
2007; Zweigenhaft, 2008) and weak correlated with U&C
(see Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003; George et al., 2007; Zweigenhaft, 2008) as most other studies report. Further, the
result of Rentfrow and Gosling (2003) and Delsing and colleagues (2008) that Extraversion is correlated with U&C
was confirmed in the male sample and by means of rating
soundfiles.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. In a new sample of 422 young German adults, Langmeyer et al. (2012) empirically retest and directly compare the correlation matrix between Big Five personality traits and music preference dimensions against the published findings of Delsing et al. (2008) in Results (Table 6) and Discussion, specifically confirming Delsing et al.'s (2008) positive Openness-R&C, Openness-I&R, and Extraversion-E&R correlations, negative Conscientiousness-I&R correlation, positive Extraversion-U&C correlation, and negative I&R-E&R intercorrelation, concluding that the results of the studies from the United States and The Netherlands also apply to the German sample. The reference list (lines 707-708) provides the exact source-backed identity without a DOI. The sole shipped row (input_row_index 683, Rentfrow & Gosling, 2003, 10.1037/0022-3514.84.6.1236) and sibling targets (George et al., 2007; Zweigenhaft, 2008) are independent studies by different author teams in different journals and populations, so report equivalence does not apply.

decision.quote: Mental health concerns on university campuses are increasing in the UK. Improving mental health literacy (MHL) for students may be a useful part of an integrated approach to effectively address these concerns. This study evaluated a previously demonstrated effective Canadian campus MHL resource in a UK student sample.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. The supplied primary source contains only the title, abstract, and unnumbered reference list, without the main text or in-text citations. While the title and abstract confirm an empirical replication evaluating the Transitions (2nd edition) Canadian campus MHL resource in a UK university sample, the reference list contains multiple plausible Canadian postsecondary MHL intervention studies—including the shipped original Kutcher, Wei, & Morgan (2016c) (input_row_index 112, 10.1177/0017896915610144), Potvin-Boucher et al. (2010), and Gilham et al. (2018)—so the available evidence cannot settle whether the retested original is already represented by shipped row 112 or is a distinct unshipped work.

decision.quote: We investigated the replicability of step count measures across two geographically distinct MS cohorts using different activity monitoring devices. Mirroring the approach used in the CA cohort ( 11 ,  12 ) study of 97 participants with MS using wrist-worn Fitbit activity monitors, we replicated key findings in the VA cohort ( 13 ) of 61 participants with MS with less severe disability, assessed using the hip-worn ActiGraph sensors.
decision.reason: Prior adjudication and state files are absent. Across the entire primary text, References 11 and 12 are never cited separately; they are always cited jointly as '( 11 ,  12 )' to refer to one single California (CA) cohort study ('In 2019, we published a foundational study to demonstrate the utility of wearable metrics in a California-based cohort [CA], using data from wrist-worn Fitbit devices to characterize step count patterns in MS patients ( 11 ,  12 )' and 'the CA cohort ( 11 ,  12 ) study of 97 participants with MS using wrist-worn Fitbit activity monitors'). Methods describes a single CA study protocol (99 MS patients recruited at UCSF between July 2015 and April 2016, n = 97 with EDSS and step count data). Reference 12 (Block et al., 2016/2017, carrying Neurology conference supplement abstract DOI 10.1212/WNL.88.16_supplement.P1.376 and baseline report metadata) and Reference 11 (Block et al., 2019, JAMA Network Open, 10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2019.0570) are preliminary/baseline and full reports of the same original UCSF CA cohort study already represented by shipped row input_row_index 587 (and sibling target_index 0).
